description:
I believe this tree may have been struck by lightning, and I think it was already dead at the time? (I think it's dead now). A few points:
1) The very long, spiraling wound seems consistent with a lightning strike, whereas it seems inconsistent with both disease and other kinds of environmental damage (eg. freeze cracks, which I don't think trees at this latitude would ever experience anyway).
2) I think there would have normally been more immediate damage had the tree been living at the time. My understanding is that what usually happens is that the lightning creates essentially a steam explosion as the sap is superheated by the bolt, which makes the wood explode and creates a deep wound on the tree. If you look at the first photo though, you can see that there's a fairly thin grey line in the middle of the wound. I believe that's the original lightning wound, and you can see that it wasn't very wide/deep, which to me suggests there was not a lot of sap which would get superheated (therefore, the tree was dead). In photo 5, you can also see that there's a part of the wound which is much narrower, and is basically just missing a bit of bark. I imagine that the original strike probably took off the bark from the tree, although I'm not sure how. Maybe it just created enough stress that it later fell off by itself?
3) Whatever the case, it's interesting to note that the original path of the lightning may have actually protected the wood, since the subsequent damage to the wood seems to mostly be localized on either side of the stripe. I don't have a great idea about how this came to be. One possibility is that the lightning literally sterilized the area, killing any fungi that were already present in the area and preventing them from rotting the wood as fast as the neighboring areas. I don't think that's terribly likely. Another possibility is that the lightning strike made the wood harder, effectively "fire-hardening" the wood by driving out the moisture and making it more difficult for organisms to damage it. A third possibility is that the lightning completely removed the bark just outside of the lightning path, but only partially separated the neighboring bark. Insects would then have colonized the areas covered with bark, but left the exposed stripe in the middle alone. 
4) However the stripe got its protection from fungi/insects though, the neighboring areas would have gotten colonized by insects (ants, termites, beetles). I think then pileated woodpeckers came along and selectively chipped away at those areas, which is why they left the central stripe alone. The mess of wood chips in the first picture is therefore a result not of the lightning strike itself, but of pileated woodpeckers (and maybe other woodpeckers as well) digging for insects.
5) I originally thought that the recent damage (all the wood chips being above the leaf litter and whatnot) indicated a recent lightning strike, but now I don't know if it is possible to date the whole sequence of events. Maybe we could get an idea by knowing how fast ants/termites are able to colonize a wound, and then measuring the width of the damage on either side of the stripe. 

Anyway, see the previous obs. for another potential lightning strike. The two trees weren't THAT far away (measuring with google earth, about 153m or 502ft), and lightning bolts often branch before hitting the ground. I wonder if the two could have been hit by the same bolt?

description:
It is the longest living non-clonal flowering plant in Eastern North America, capable of living over 650 years.

The limbs of these trees often deteriorate early, and the decayed holes make excellent dens for squirrels, raccoons, Virginia opossums, as well as nesting sites for honeybees.

Black gum trees are also known as bee gums because early settlers used the hollow trunks of the trees to house their beehives. They are highly favored by honey producers for creating a light and mild-tasting honey.

They are an important food source for many migrating birds in the fall. Its early color change is thought to attract birds to the available fruit, which ripen before other speices. The sour fruits are eagerly sought by many kinds of birds, including: American robin, Swainson's thrush, gray-cheeked thrush, hermit thrush, wood thrush, northern cardinal, northern mockingbird, blue jay, red-bellied woodpecker, yellow-bellied sapsucker, northern flicker, pileated woodpecker, eastern phoebe, brown thrasher, eastern bluebird, scarlet tanager, gray catbird, cedar waxwing, and American crow.

The wood is heavy, hard, cross-grained, and difficult to split, especially after drying. This resistance to splitting led to its use for making mauls, pulleys, wheel hubs, agricultural rollers, bowls, and paving blocks. The wood is also used for pallets, rough floors, pulpwood, and firewood. Since its very tough and resistant to wear, it has been used for shuttles in weaving. Because it is resistant to wear and very readily accepts creosote-based preservatives it is considered to be a premier wood for making railroad ties. The wood's resistance to wear and some acids has led to its use as factory flooring.

Black gum is great for whittling because it can hold fine details, paints well, and doesn't "fuzz up"  like basswood.

The tree has a large number of branches that all grow downwards, forming an overall pyramidal shape. The leaves are entire with a slight tip at the top, and grow in a whorl at the terminal point of the branch. Some leaves have small galls present on their surface that appear like green pimples, and the appearance of the leaves look smooth and wet. The flowers of the tree are small, green, and grow from the terminal point of the branch and between the leaves. They grow at the end of their own individual stems and in large clusters. The bark is a dark tan or light brown color, and has vertical grooves that almost appear parallel with one another.
